reviews.review: Interesting, unique, tight, enjoyable. Somewhere in the vicinity of Hypnospace Outlaw and Her Story. Extremely tight plot with very few holes, a reliable interface and control, and a compelling style. Marred by three notable flaws. First, the writing (not the plot; just the writing itself) is fairly stilted at times. Only two characters really have distinctive voices; the rest tend to just blend together, especially in crowded scenes. Second, there are a few times where the result of submitting datachunks is unclear, or conveys a different message than you intended to send. A minor nuisance, but it annoyed me a couple times. Finally, and most prevalent: an extremely common repeated bug whereby the mouseover tooltips on datachunks simply don't appear. Restarting the game is the only way to fix it, and rarely for long. I think in the handful of hours I played this game, I restarted it about 30 times because of this.

I came here having tried Orwell a few years ago and didn't take to it... Then I played "Return of the Obra Dinn" and was so entranced by it I searched for "Game like..." and this came up, so I went back and started over.

I'll just say that this game is NOTHING like "Return of the Obra Dinn".    It feels like the "Walking Simulator" of detective games. You don't 'detect' so to speak, more than you just walk through scads and scads of documents and photographs, and picking out important pieces that are pre-highlighted for you.  Occasionally you get to make a moral / ambiguous choice between two things with far too little / ambiguous information.   This is kind of the point of the game... To show how easily we can be led down a path of conclusion based on scant evidence... Is the player 'aware' enough of the situation to select the correct interpretation.  Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not.

Where Orwell falls down is that the consequence of what you pull out of the documentation isn't always clear.   You can be pulling out loads of stuff, with the occasional snide / snippy remark from your 'advisor', with no noticeable progress in the game.  Then all of a sudden, you pick something and *BOOM*  the whole world spins on its axis, and you suddenly get more context, albeit too late.

Now, as I said, the 'late information binding' thang is the whole Orwell shtick, but it's really s****g annoying when you're playing.  It's only in the end game, that the whole POINT of the game becomes clear and you realise that the annoyance you're feeling has a purpose.

Then the game offers you a moral choice...   Carry on, or rebel.  For me, the decision was pretty clear cut, but it didn't look like it had much effect, tbh.     And that's the other big issue, is that you're never sure if you chose correctly, wrongly, or your choice made no major difference.  Some might say this adds 'replayability', but to be honest, I don't think I can be bothered clicking through dozens of semi-meaningless PDFs for another 10 hours to choose different outcomes to test the theory....

Get it if you like making your own deductions and choices.

"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" seems content to repeat what books and movies have said more eloquently.  It also falls below the dollar per hour metric (it can be completed within 5 hours).

The gameplay is simple and involves clicking through fake internet websites, blogs, and chat logs to collect bits of information (a process that can easily become tedious).

So the appeal is obviously the story, but for $9.99, you're better off buying a copy of George Orwell's 1984, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World instead. This game is nothing more than a shallow summary of the themes explored in depth by those literary works.

This is a visual novel along the same lines as A Lost Phone. Everything you might want to click is almost always highlighted with a red box, star, or a red/blue/grey page icon by the resource's entry in your listing, so getting lost and missing things is tricky. The main challenge is deciding what to submit as evidence and what not to. In my first playthrough, I submitted everything I found, just to see what it did, but in later playthroughs I was more discerning, shaping the narrative to my own ends.

The story is a fairly good one about omnipresent surveillance, though unlikely to give chills to anyone who knows the NSA exists. The system in the game is *ridiculously* hobbled compared to real-world ones: they can only spy on people they have permission to; they can only view documents and devices that have been revealed through the investigation; they can't communicate; they can't correct any ambiguities with better information; they can't... etc etc. It's a deliberately-hobbled system, for reasons made clear during the game, but it does have the advantage that, technologically at least, they have access to *everything, immediately*.

All possible endings are morally ambivalent, so there's arguably no "good" or "bad" ending.

While there's an option to speed up phone calls and messaging, it only works a little bit, speeding it up from "interminable crawl" to "this is bearable, but still painful to replay". There are some minor bugs about the highlighting of things, particularly where mouseovering things doesn't always show the tooltip describing its effects. But the tooltips aren't critical, you can guess from context.

100%-ing the achievements it is a bit of a pain for completionists, since you have to play through it 2.5 times, but it's entirely possible, and the game repays another playthrough or two because there are multiple endings and outcomes for most of the characters, depending whether you play pro-government, pro-activist, or somewhere between.

[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

If you're a fan of games that put you in a Detective-like role requiring the use of deduction, then you should find this game entertaining. It's a point-and-click style game where you build profiles on suspects in an attempt to solve a crime. The entire interface is like a work computer and you are able to explore news articles, social media profiles, phone calls, emails, and even browse through suspect's personal devices to pull relevant "data chunks" into their appropriate profiles. The majority of the game plays at a pretty chill pace, though there are a few points where quick actions (such as pulling data during a live phone call) may be required to get the outcome you're hoping for. Overall great writing, interesting characters, nice visual interface, and replayability to see how different choices affect the game's outcome.

Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

Orwell is really good.

It starts as a simple "first day on the job" where you're discovering the world the game takes place in, and the people you're going to learn everything about.

But then the morality of what is in front of you hits. You are gathering a staggeringly terrifying amount of data, literally everything you find about people, through their phones, computers, emails, you even hack into their accounts.
At that point, you either decide to play along the system's rules, follow orders and send people in prison, regardless of the fact they're actually guilty or not, because [b]you made them guilty anyways[/b], or you start to use the scary amount of information collected to actively work against the machine, to right the wrongs of a government that doesn't shy away from considering [b]any[/b] of it's citizens as a threat if that's what it takes to keep the machine going.
A fabricated justification to secretly introduce mass surveillance, a system in which everyone and anyone is a target and where constructed truths that profit the top of the food chain are invaluable in the eyes of the people that operate that very system.


That aside, the group that the game centers around, Thought, is fascinating, and there are many twists and turn in their interactions that will keep you wondering how each piece of the puzzle can fit with the others. Some of these characters are incredibly well written and others are complete mysteries.

The gameplay is mostly browsing documents and sliding data into a box. From which set of data you collect (and which you either by mistake or on purpose, don't collect), different things will happen and you will be able to affect the direction of the story over the course of 5 days.

Visually, it is very clean and neat, almost cold, and it's probably on purpose. Your character is using a software that is "the most powerful mass surveillance tool ever made". It's not here to be pretty, it's here to be efficient.
 The interface is simple and easy to grasp. The "geometrical" style of the pictures in various documents is a nice touch.

The music is mostly just ambience, you don't even notice it until you do, which in my opinion, is just how it should be for this type of game.

At first I wasn't sure if i would like the game, as some story driven games I like, but others I don't. However, I very quickly found out that I was going to like the game, and I enjoyed it the whole way through. Orwell pushes you to use processes of investigation to try and prevent tragedy using a sophisticated surveillance system. The game mechanics are actually very fun, as you have to do some detective work to find connections by eavesdropping on what people say on the phone, over text, through their bank account purchases, social media accounts, etc. You even get to the point where you have to help provide information to a SWAT team during a raid, for example. Your actions have consequences. I got a few things wrong, and some people died...

This game is... strange in a wonderful way. You basically spend the entire game crawling through phone records, text messages, and webpages, putting together profiles of people. You get to decide what's "important" and what isn't, and see what happens based on those choices.

The plot is excellent and relevant, and despite having horrifically bad graphics (which is intended), it doesn't actually detract from the experience.

I keep coming back to this game.

There is not much branching narrative or deeper exploration to be had past the first play, but there is something immersive about feeling like a cog in a much larger dystopian machine. It speaks of the information we offer freely on the internet, and how a uncaring but well-intentioned governmental implement can mismanage things even when they are being careful and methodical.

Each story beat is another day, so I take measured day-by-day experiences, logging out at the end of my shift and logging in the next day to continue my work. There's some meditation to the practice, but it is paired with the stress that every choice you make could have irreparable consequences.

Orwell is a fascinating narrative game that's well-written and full of twists. You play as a government investigator trying to uncover who is behind a terrorist plot. The story slowly unravels itself through the panopticon of documents and conversations that you must scan through for information. One playthrough takes around 3-5 hours, though there is some replayability because the things you choose (or omit) to investigate could change the course of the events that follow. If you're a sharp-minded person who loves discovering patterns and non-linear storytelling, this sleuthing game is for you. I thoroughly enjoyed it!

I bought this game with the surveillance pack while it was on sale, and boy do I regret it. This game has a fun idea, but that's about it.

First, the gameplay is very disappointing and tiring. You don't have to look for anything, as everything is highlighted. There are few choices, and you only need to click and drag on the side. Every time you put a clue into the "database," you get interrupted by a guy either mocking you for adding an "useless" piece of information or explaining what you just added and how it helps in the story line. You can never be wrong putting a clue because you get corrected or the guy confirms that the clue is correct and explains it, it just feels like you're on a tutorial mode the entire game. Also, the fact that you can't change the clues you added or erase them is a pain. You can prevent that by hovering over a clue to see what it will add, but I didn't know that because this game bugged so much that the information didn't appear until mid-game.

The story is simple and I found it okay. It has some plot twists, etc., but it is very long for its worth. There are multiple endings, and just to get one is very confusing because it feels like every possible ending is being thrown at you and you have to pick one. I already forced myself to finish one, and I don't think I will launch this game again.

Overall, if you're looking for a small investigation game or want to feel like a detective, pass on this game. It would have been a great mobile game, but is tedious on PC.

An intelligent and enjoyable yet chilling game that highlights the bias of media outlets and the danger of out-of-context information. With multiple plays, you see the consequences of even small decisions, which encourages thorough thought in each following decision.
Very easy and fast to play - one playthrough is only a few hours. I recommend playing the game multiple times with different decisions made each playthrough, as it gives you a good view of all the potential endings for the game.

You don't have to agree with the characters to see the point in their respective battles. This game really helps give perspective and an overall respect for the differing views of other people.

I also recommend following the story through with the sequel game, Orwell: Ignorance is Strength, which uses a chosen save file of Orwell to directly continue the story.

Solid detective/mystery game with a narrative that adapts to your choices. Especially towards the ending of the game, things get really interesting and confusing in a mentally challenging way. I recommend it if you're looking for a cognitive experience.

The plot itself also weaves in clashing ideas about surveillance and security very well.
